\chapter{What?}
\label{ch:zh-shenme}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write \zh{什} and \zh{么}, ask \zh{什么} to mean what, use it on its own to get something repeated, judge that it is blunt with a stranger, and I know its two characters are there for sound rather than meaning.}

The first exchange in the track that goes wrong -- one speaker mishears -- and the first the reader can repair, which matters more than another memorised line because it is what keeps a conversation alive when the Mandarin runs out.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[shén]{\zh{什} — both halves are old news}

\label{lesson:ZH-W09-shen}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{亻}, the standing person — two strokes, at the left edge of a block.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{什}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Four strokes}, and after \zh{我} that will feel like a rest.

\textbf{\zh{什} is \zh{亻} beside \zh{十}}, and you have met both:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{亻}} you wrote in the very first word of this book, standing at the left of \zh{你}
  \item \textbf{\zh{十}} you drew inside \zh{早}, underneath the sun
\end{itemize}

1. \textbf{\zh{亻}'s falling stroke}, from the upper centre down to the left 2. \textbf{\zh{亻}'s vertical}, straight down to the baseline 3. \textbf{\zh{十}'s horizontal}, left to right 4. \textbf{\zh{十}'s vertical}, down \emph{through} that horizontal

Three pen lifts.

\textbf{Finish \zh{亻} before starting \zh{十}} — left before right, the oldest habit you have. And inside \zh{十}, horizontal before vertical, because the two cross.

A note on \zh{十}, since this is the second time it has turned up without being taught. It is the character for \textbf{ten}, and you still do not need to write it on its own. When it eventually arrives as a character in its own right, you will already have drawn it twice.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{亻} alone, then \zh{什} — the second half is two strokes
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{什} again, saying \textquotedblleft{}person, then ten\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shén} — rising
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which stroke of \zh{十} comes first? (\textbf{The horizontal} — the two cross.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[me]{\zh{么} — three strokes, and one of them turns}

\label{lesson:ZH-W09-me}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{什}. Person on the left, ten on the right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{么}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Three strokes}, and the middle one does the work:

1. a short \textbf{falling stroke} at the top, down to the left 2. a second \textbf{falling stroke} down-left that \textbf{turns without lifting} and \textbf{sweeps right} along the base 3. a \textbf{dot}, pressed down-right

Two pen lifts.

Stroke 2 is one movement, not two: down-left, then a turn, then out to the right. Lift in the middle of it and you have written something else. You have handled this before — the frame of \zh{再}, the leg of \zh{见} — and the instinct is the same: \textbf{the pen turns, the stroke does not end.}

The dot goes last, as it did in \zh{我}.

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{么}} is \emph{me} — and that is the whole pronunciation. \textbf{No tone mark, because it has no tone.}

You met neutral syllables inside words, where \zh{上} and \zh{字} gave their tones up. \zh{么} is different: it is neutral in the dictionary, standing alone. Some characters simply never carry a tone, and this is your first.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{么} — and keep stroke 2 unbroken through its turn
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{me} — short, light, flat, no shape to it at all
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does this character have no tone mark? (\textbf{Because it has no tone}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[shénme]{\zh{什么} — what}

\label{lesson:ZH-C09-shenme}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{me}. Short and flat, no tone at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\zh{什么}} \emph{shénme} — \textbf{what}.

\emph{shén} rises; \emph{me} is light and toneless behind it. Both characters are ones you have just written.

This one is different in kind from everything before it. \zh{你好}, \zh{是}, \zh{不是}, \zh{再见}, \zh{早上好}, \zh{我是} — every one of those \textbf{gives} something. \textbf{\zh{什么} asks.} It is the first word in this book whose job is to get something back from the other person.

Here the honest note this book owes you: the two halves of \zh{什么} do \textbf{not} add up the way \zh{再见}'s did. \zh{什} and \zh{么} are here for sound, not for meaning. Trying to read \textquotedblleft{}ten-person\textquotedblright{} out of it would be inventing a story, and you would be worse off for believing it. Some words are built; some are just words.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\zh{什么}?} by itself means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}What?\textquotedblright{}} — the thing you say when you did not catch what someone said. That is real, everyday Mandarin and it is the most useful thing you can do with this word today.

One caution, because register matters and this book would rather tell you than let you find out. A bare \textbf{\zh{什么}?} is \textbf{blunt} — closer to English \textquotedblleft{}What?\textquotedblright{} than to \textquotedblleft{}Sorry?\textquotedblright{}. Between friends it is unremarkable. To a stranger, or to anyone you would be careful with, it lands harder than you intend, and Mandarin has gentler ways to ask for a repeat that need words you do not have yet.

So: use it, and know what it weighs.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shénme} — rising, then light
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{shénme?} as a question, as though you missed something
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{什么}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do the two halves of \zh{什么} add up to its meaning? (\textbf{No} — they are there for sound.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — when you did not catch it}

\label{lesson:ZH-C09-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{shénme} — rising, then light.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Two people meet. One of them mishears. Fill both gaps with real names.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{早上好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zǎoshang hǎo} — good morning.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{早上好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zǎoshang hǎo} — good morning.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{我是} …
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{wǒ shì …} — I am …
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{什么}?
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{shénme?} — what?
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{我是} …
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{wǒ shì …} — I am … (said again, slower)
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{再见}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zàijiàn} — goodbye.
\end{quote}

That fourth line is the point of the chapter. Until now every exchange in this book has gone perfectly, which is not what conversations do. \textbf{B did not catch it, said so, and got it repeated.} That is a repair, and being able to make one is worth more than another memorised phrase — it is what keeps a conversation alive when your Mandarin runs out.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — and the question you still cannot ask}]
You can greet by the hour, say who you are, ask for a repeat when you miss something, and leave.

The gap named last chapter is still open, and it is worth being precise about what changed. You now have \textbf{\zh{什么}}, the \emph{what} of \textquotedblleft{}what is your name?\textquotedblright{} — but not yet the rest of that sentence. Both halves of the question exist in Mandarin; this book has handed you one of them. The other needs a character the font in this book cannot yet print, which is a dull reason, and a true one.

So the honest position: \textbf{\zh{什么} is a question word you can use today} in the ways above, and a piece of a question you will finish later.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both parts, including the mishearing
  \item \textbf{shénme?} three times — once to a friend, once to a stranger, and notice it is the same word and not the same act
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is a bare \zh{什么}? gentle or blunt? (\textbf{Blunt} — fine with friends, heavy with strangers.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
